## 2026-10-03 hook-free follow-up requested by ct

### Conclusion and upstream intent

The per-worktree split observed in the original spike is a consequence of Hive's custom bootstrap helper, not the normal br 0.7.4 worktree workflow. With no Git hooks and no database override, fresh linked worktrees resolve the complete DB/config/JSONL family to the primary checkout. Cwd can remain the code worktree while tracker authority is primary. A main-checkout colony would immediately see new spawns, claims, and closures in this topology, without a commit/merge handoff. This refines the original rationale: worktree-local invisible queues describe today's customized Hive topology, not a general br limitation. Explicit per-repository --db routing for the system-wide daemon remains appropriate, especially with already-initialized stores or inherited overrides.

This is deliberate upstream behavior. Maintainer confirmation on PR #429 (https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust/pull/429) explains that discovering the tracked snapshot as a workspace rebuilt a private DB from possibly stale JSONL and split state. The fix routes a linked worktree with no local DB/redirect to primary; existing local DBs and explicit redirects remain supported choices. Matching installed source: https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust/blob/3956ebb8417414eba883e2446a4cefafa07d0b75/src/config/mod.rs#L322-L398.

Hooks themselves are allowed: upstream SYNC_SAFETY.md documents an optional custom flush-and-stage hook. The problem is the specific Hive policy: .husky/beads-sync uses git rev-parse --show-toplevel, then explicit --db <worktree>/.beads/beads.db and, when absent, --no-auto-import sync --merge --force-jsonl. That bootstraps the very private store upstream default discovery avoids. Hive's sync.auto_import=false and sync.auto_flush=false separately replace normal automatic publication/import with manual/hook responsibility.

### Recommended no-hook runbook

Authority: the installed br robot-docs guide, reproduced verbatim in the experiment transcript, plus the README and SYNC_SAFETY.md at the installed release commit. Sources:
- https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust/blob/3956ebb8417414eba883e2446a4cefafa07d0b75/src/cli/commands/robot_docs.rs
- https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust/blob/3956ebb8417414eba883e2446a4cefafa07d0b75/README.md
- https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/beads_rust/blob/3956ebb8417414eba883e2446a4cefafa07d0b75/docs/SYNC_SAFETY.md

1. Initialize br once in the primary checkout. Keep normal sync.auto_import/auto_flush defaults enabled. Do not initialize or explicitly bootstrap a private database in each linked worktree unless independent workspace trackers are intentional. Verify selection with br where --json.
2. Use br from the code cwd. Mutations normally update SQLite and auto-flush the selected workspace's issues.jsonl; ordinary commands check changed local JSONL and auto-import when safe. Neither phase runs Git or transports branch state.
3. At completion, br close <id> --reason 'Completed: <proof>' --actor <harness> --json, then br sync --flush-only. Stage code and .beads changes explicitly with Git; commit/push remain operator/agent actions. No routine merge, force, or allow-stale flag is required for ordinary export.
4. After Git pull/merge has delivered changed JSONL, inspect br sync --status --json and use br sync --import-only for an explicit import. With default settings an ordinary issue read also performs the safe startup import. Resolve Git conflict markers before importing.
5. Reserve br sync --merge for independently changed DB and JSONL. It requires the saved .beads/beads.base.jsonl and explicit handling of semantic conflicts. Auto-import is not proof that a merge base exists. In this clean imported-clone fixture, sync --merge initially refused missing base (exit 6); an ordinary final flush brought exported DB and JSONL into agreement, then unforced sync --merge established the base before divergence. After a no-auto-flush DB title edit plus a different issue's upstream JSONL title edit, normal startup warned/skipped import, and explicit unforced sync --merge preserved both active issues. This is a controlled checkpoint demonstration, not permission to force an export over arbitrary drift.

Worktree staging caveat: br flush from a linked worktree exports PRIMARY JSONL, while git add .beads there stages that worktree's tracked snapshot. The generic runbook's same-checkout staging example therefore must be applied at the selected tracker workspace root. Our tested no-copy handoff was: commit feature code in its worktree, run br sync --flush-only and git add .beads / git commit at primary, then integrate the feature through normal Git merge. Primary tracker records survived integration. Trying git add <primary>/.beads/issues.jsonl from the linked worktree was refused (exit 128 outside repository). A requirement to package all tracker/code edits into the same branch commit needs a deliberate Git handoff design; the guide does not solve that automatically, and blind snapshot copying is not recommended.

### Observed comparison

- Vanilla defaults + no hooks: nested worktree root, deep subdirectory, second nested worktree and sibling worktree all resolve primary DB/JSONL. A worktree create is immediately visible from primary/other worktrees and exports primary JSONL only; no private DB appears. A claim becomes visible everywhere and a different actor's second claim is refused (exit 4). Closure is visible without Git transport.
- No hooks + Hive's autosync-off config: still one primary DB and immediate visibility, but no automatic JSONL export. Explicit sync --flush-only exports primary JSONL. Thus the config flags do not create separate stores.
- Same fixture + explicitly invoking the unchanged Hive helper once (still no installed/executed Git hooks): it creates a private DB from the older checkout JSONL and subsequent ordinary discovery chooses it. A newer primary-only bead is absent there (exit 3), a local addition is absent from primary (exit 3), and the same seed is successfully claimed by codex in primary and pi in the worktree.
- Separate clone: initially no ignored DB; sync --import-only initializes its own store from local JSONL. Hook-free pull transports JSONL only. An opt-out read sees old state; a default read auto-imports, and explicit status/import also makes the next transported bead visible. Clone databases remain separate, as intended.

### Recommendation and remaining policy decision

For a repository-wide bee/colony queue, align with upstream shared-primary discovery and normal auto-sync defaults; use explicit --db for daemon-owned routing. Replace the per-worktree bootstrap/reconciliation policy through a dedicated implementation change only if ct chooses this direction. An optional later hook can automate an approved flush/staging workflow, but must not accidentally create a private worktree DB.

Removing hooks alone will not migrate existing initialized worktrees: upstream deliberately preserves their local stores, and Hive's disabled automatic sync would still apply. Reconcile existing DB-only state and plan canonical JSONL transport before changing authority. No production code, Git configuration, or policy file was changed in this follow-up. ct highlighted a gap in the preceding recommendation: shared-primary auto-flush immediately changes primary issues.jsonl even when br is invoked from a feature worktree. This dirties canonical main and blocks Honeycomb. Simply committing the tracker also does not make default fresh_canonical operations ready: main's HEAD must be an ancestor of origin/main, so an unpublished local tracker commit is refused until pushed.

Installed/current Hive Honeycomb configuration: add policy fresh_canonical; finish strategy squash, push true, remove_worktree true, delete_branch true. Disposable tests retained the relevant fresh_canonical + squash gates but set push/cleanup false so the probe could inspect retained worktrees; every push was explicitly to disposable local bare origin. add calls used no --base or --base-current override. Source: lib/honeycomb/src/application/branches.ts:68-95 requires clean canonical checkout on default branch and HEAD ancestor of origin/default; lib/honeycomb/src/commands/finish.ts:80-113 validates target before integration and pushes only after integration. finish's eventual push cannot cure a pre-existing unpublished tracker commit because the readiness check happens first. Existing branches or explicit base overrides have different add paths; this finding is specifically the user's default fresh_canonical workflow. The earlier no-hook harness used --base-current and was not evidence about this default guard.

### Exactly when files and Git dirtiness change

SQLite is ignored runtime state. A task mutation changes the selected DB immediately, but that alone does not dirty Git. JSONL is tracked interchange state.
- Shared-primary with default auto_flush=true: successful task create/claim/notes/close normally exports primary JSONL immediately. If exported bytes differ from the staged/committed version, primary is dirty; the feature's tracked JSONL stays unchanged.
- Shared-primary with auto_flush=false: task changes remain in ignored primary DB and are visible immediately to all callers using that DB. Primary JSONL remains unchanged and canonical Git remains clean until an explicit sync export/checkpoint.
- br sync --flush-only exports the selected DB; if bytes differ, primary becomes dirty. It neither stages nor commits nor pushes. Re-running with no changed bytes need not dirty anything.
- git add stages the file; staged-but-uncommitted changes still fail Honeycomb's porcelain cleanliness check.
- git commit records those bytes and makes the checkout clean (assuming no other edits), but HEAD is now ahead of origin and fresh_canonical still refuses.
- git push publishes the commit; subsequent fetch sees matching origin state and restores readiness if no additional changes arose.
- A successful Git merge or squash integration may change tracked JSONL but records the resulting bytes in its commit. Changing a file as part of a committed checkout update is not inherently Git dirtiness. Conflicted or uncommitted merges are different.
- With no Git hook, Git merge does not update SQLite itself. If incoming committed JSONL changes need to enter the selected DB, a normal br command can auto-import when safe, or use explicit sync --import-only. If the DB has pending independent changes, use the established-base sync --merge procedure from the earlier follow-up; ordinary startup can warn/skip instead of importing.

```mermaid

  Local --> Blocked["Fresh canonical still refuses"]
  Local -- push --> Published["Main clean and published"]

  Integrated -- close task with auto flush --> DirtyAgain["Main JSONL changes again"]
```

G04-G11: tracker commit cleared main's dirty status but made it one commit ahead; default add and finish returned exit 10 reason non_ff_canonical. Push to disposable origin restored add readiness. Squash finish then integrated the code and preserved the primary's already-published tracker addition, even though the feature branch's committed JSONL snapshot lacked that bead. This is ordinary three-way Git merge behavior: an unchanged older snapshot does not overwrite a change made on the other side. Both sides actually editing the same JSONL line can conflict; this case did not test such a conflict. After the integrated main was pushed, br close from the retained feature worktree exported a closed status to primary JSONL, dirtied main again, and blocked the next default add. Commit+push of completion restored it.

Conceptual Git comparison: common ancestor has task=open; main commits task=in_progress; feature changes only code and retains task=open. Integration keeps task=in_progress plus feature code, rather than treating the feature's older file as a replacement snapshot. Do not manually copy that old snapshot onto primary.

### Example 3: shared live DB with deliberate publication

P01-P05: a separate fixture initialized br once at primary, with sync.auto_import=true and sync.auto_flush=false, and no hook/private worktree bootstrap. Worktree br create updated the shared DB and was immediately visible from primary while both Git roots remained clean. Another default Honeycomb add succeeded. Explicit br sync --flush-only from the worktree then exported primary JSONL and dirtied main; add refused until those bytes were committed and pushed at primary. Thus sharing runtime task authority and scheduling JSONL publication are independent choices.

This revises the preceding blanket recommendation to restore both auto-sync defaults: for Hive's clean-main workflow, shared-primary runtime DB plus deliberate JSONL publication is a candidate to evaluate. Keep automatic import enabled if desired, and coordinate publication/import around concurrent agents and incoming Git state. With auto-flush disabled, pending live DB state is not yet Git-published/backed up through JSONL. A dedicated tracker workspace is another architectural option, but was not implemented or tested here. Existing initialized worktrees still require reconciliation before any authority change.

Current Hive's contrast: its helpers create per-worktree stores and disable both automatic phases. A normal task update changes ignored worktree DB; pre-commit exports/stages local JSONL with the code commit, while post-merge reconciles primary. That lets code and tracker travel through a branch commit and keeps routine worker task updates from dirtying main, but yields separate claim/visibility domains. The helper solves a Git publication problem while introducing a coordination tradeoff; it is not simply forbidden by upstream. No policy has been changed.

title: Record: design conversation transcript (agent identity and bees)
description:
# Design conversation: agent identity and bees

Verbatim user/assistant dialogue from Claude Code session `5886da0d-8ce1-4f10-9909-8d0c8543094e` (2026-10-02), extracted by Pi (deepseek-flash) with the claude-session-introspection skill from the harness dialogue log. Tool calls, thinking, system reminders and background-task notifications are excluded. Turn markers are numbered `# [n] User` / `# [n] Assistant`; `##` headings inside turns are part of the messages. Turns 12–14 include earlier, abandoned wordings of the final request and one assistant reply from that abandoned attempt; they are kept as recorded. Second opinions from gpt-6-astra are summarised in the assistant turns, not reproduced. The conversation ends at the request that created this record.

# [1] User

i need to add identity to agents, this will allow bead audit trails to track the actor making changes

if you look through /Users/ct/dev/projects/millhouse.spool/spools/harnesses/plugins/millstrand-identity/README.md i had agents build this out before in another system, but i think it was a total mess and massively over complicated

help me walk through a way we could implement this in a way harnesses can use. It almost certainly needs to be a harness hook, like a claude code sessionStart hook (codex has the same) or pi which has a lower level typescript api

this gives usually gives us the model and effort, which we can use to drive env vars (if the harness lets us, which claude and pi do), and we can also pick up any environment variables set from outside, and finally we can inject the identity into the model's system prompt (helps insure it's clear and not just normal user prompt)

there are two ways an agent is launched, one is natively, e.g the desktop apps for claude/codex, the clis directly in a tty; the second is via some automation, e.g @scripts/beads-loop.ts which can much more easily set any needed env vars

for case 2, and agent might simply recieve NAME, MODEL, EFFORT, and then set its prompt. THis means we'd want some automation to mint the friendly identity first before passing it in
for case 1, the harness hook would need to mint the friendly identity (passing in model and effort from the hook if provided) and then pass this into the system prompt (and if the harness supports it, inject these as ENV vars so the agent doesn't need to keep typing them, as BD_ACTOR sets --actor automatically for example)

thoughts, you can use claude code session hooks as an example of how we'd build this

# [1] Assistant

I agree the old plugin was over-built: about 3,000 lines, a server registration callback, run references, Git workspace gates and conformance fixtures. Most of that existed only to keep identity state. If the name is derived from the session ID instead of stored, all of that state goes away.

## The core idea

Each harness hook is a thin adapter around one shared pure function. Automation only sets env vars. The hook always does the rendering.

```
 case 2 (automation)                    case 1 (native)
 beads-loop: mintName(uuid)             nothing set
 → HIVE_AGENT_NAME etc. in child env           │
            │                                  │
            └──────────────┬───────────────────┘
                           ▼
   harness hook: payload {session_id, model, effort?} + process.env
                           │
                 resolveIdentity()   ← pure, @hive/shared
                           │
              ┌────────────┴────────────┐
              ▼                         ▼
     export env (if supported)    inject into the prompt
     BD_ACTOR, HIVE_AGENT_*       "You are amber-otter …"
```

**Precedence rules:**

| field | order |
|---|---|
| name | env `HIVE_AGENT_NAME` → `mintName(session_id)` |
| model | value the hook sees → env `HIVE_AGENT_MODEL` → `unknown` |
| effort | value the hook sees → env `HIVE_AGENT_EFFORT` → `unknown` |
| `BD_ACTOR` | env, if set explicitly → derived from the above |

`mintName(seed)` hashes the seed into an adjective-noun pair from a word list. Because it's deterministic, resume, clear and compact all produce the same name again. That means no state file, no registry, and the hook can run as often as the harness likes.

## What each harness can do

| | Claude Code | Codex | Pi |
|---|---|---|---|
| hook | `SessionStart` command | `SessionStart` command | extension: `session_start` and `before_agent_start` |
| model | `model` in the payload | `model` in the payload ✓ | `ctx.model` |
| effort | ⚠️ probably not in the payload (needs checking) | ✗ not in the input schema | thinking level ✓ |
| env injection | `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` ✓ | ✗ (case 2 only, through inherited env) | change `process.env` ✓ |
| prompt | `additionalContext` (arrives as a system reminder, not the true system prompt) | `additionalContext` → developer message | real `systemPrompt` ✓ |
| stable seed | `session_id` | `session_id` (also `CODEX_THREAD_ID` in its shells) | session ID |

I checked the Codex row against the vendored `codex-rs/hooks/src/schema.rs`. The SessionStart input only has `session_id, cwd, model, permission_mode, source`, and the output only accepts `additionalContext`.

Two gaps follow from this:
- **Codex launched natively can't set env vars.** The injected context has to tell the agent to pass `--actor <name>` on every call. When the loop launches Codex, `BD_ACTOR` is already inherited by its shells, so this is fine.
- **Claude Code's true system prompt** can only be set with `--append-system-prompt`, which automation can pass at launch. A natively launched session gets `additionalContext`, which I think is clear enough.

## Suggested layout

```
lib/shared/src/identity.ts              # mintName, resolveIdentity, toEnv, renderPrompt (pure, tested)
lib/colony/src/hooks/claude.ts          # stdin JSON → writes CLAUDE_ENV_FILE + prints additionalContext
lib/colony/src/hooks/codex.ts           # stdin JSON → prints additionalContext (adds --actor guidance)
lib/colony/src/pi/identity.ts           # Pi extension: sets env + system prompt
scripts/beads-loop.ts                   # mintName(randomUUID()) → env for the spawned process
```

`colony` ("CLI abstraction over providers") seems the natural home for the adapters. Both packages are still empty scaffolds, so nothing has to move. Each adapter would be about 20–40 lines.

## Decisions to make

1. **What `BD_ACTOR` looks like.** br stores a single string, so model and effort only reach the audit trail if they're encoded in it. Options:
   - `amber-otter`: short, but you lose model and effort.
   - `claude/opus-5-5/high/amber-otter`: greppable, readable from coarse to fine. **I'd go with this one.**
   - Name only in `BD_ACTOR`, with model and effort in `--append-notes`: noisy.

   This replaces the CLAUDE.md rule that the actor is just the harness name, so CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md need updating to match.
2. **How Claude effort is read.** The options are to verify whether the payload or env exposes it, to read `effortLevel` from the settings chain, or to accept `unknown` for native sessions. I can have this checked against the docs.
3. **Gating.** I'd drop the `.millstrand` and Git gate entirely. Then the hook works everywhere and only says something when `br` is relevant, or it can run unconditionally because it's cheap.

## Related topics, if you want me to expand
- **Subagents:** Claude Task subagents share the parent's `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE`, so they would inherit the parent's actor. Codex has a separate `SubagentStart` hook.
- **Plugin packaging:** shipping the hooks as Claude and Codex plugins versus listing them in repo `.claude/settings.json` and `.codex/hooks.json`.
- **Word-list source:** pick one existing tool, such as `unique-names-generator`, or ship about 100 words inline.

If you're happy with this, I can turn it into a bead with child beads (shared core, then the three adapters, then the loop) before building anything.

# [2] User

so effort and model are best effort metadata, i don't need them if they aren't there; that said model has a place in a bead:

```
      

<pasted_content id="20b0">
--harness <HARNESS>
          Tier 1 attribution: harness identifier (env: BR_HARNESS). Recorded only [env: BR_HARNESS=]
      --model <MODEL>
          Tier 1 attribution: model identifier (env: BR_MODEL). Recorded only [env: BR_MODEL=]
</pasted_content id="20b0">

```

so we can set thos env vars if possible.

the other thing i am considering is a registry, e.g a simple toml file that gives aliases,

```toml
[[agent]]
name = "scout"
description = "fast recon agent for finding specific parts of a codebase"
systemPrompt = "focus on readonly search as per your request"
cli = "claude"
argv = "--model haiku"

[[agent]]
name = "oracle"
description = "smart advisor agent"
systemPrompt = "utalise chepaer agents to help you explore and answer questions with thorough detail. Utalise bash but in a readonly fasion"
cli = "codex"
argv = "--model gpt-astra"
```

so this could provide additional info to an agent as well as identity depending on what was set. It wouldn't work for native spawned agents, but that is unavoidable. We would want this as a label if possible on the bead, likely more useful under the harness field, e.g `claude:scout` etc

# [2] Assistant

br already has a slot for the alias. Besides `BR_HARNESS` and `BR_MODEL` there is a third tier-1 field:

```
--agent-name <NAME>   Tier 1 attribution: agent name (env: BR_AGENT_NAME). Recorded only
```

## Where each value goes

| env | value | native | via automation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BD_ACTOR` | friendly name, e.g. `amber-otter` | minted from `session_id` | minted by the launcher |
| `BR_AGENT_NAME` | registry alias, e.g. `scout` | unset | from the registry |
| `BR_HARNESS` | `claude` / `codex` / `pi` | hard-coded in each adapter | from the registry's `cli` |
| `BR_MODEL` | model ID | from the hook payload, if present | from the registry |
| *(prompt only)* | effort | from the hook, if present | from the registry |

With these fields, `BD_ACTOR` can stay just the friendly name. That settles last turn's question about how to format the actor.

**Alias field:** I'd use `BR_AGENT_NAME=scout` and keep `BR_HARNESS=claude` unmixed, rather than `claude:scout`. Every field holds one thing. Since all of them are "recorded only", nothing filters on either form, so the choice only affects how the trail reads. If you still prefer `claude:scout`, it's a one-line change in `toEnv`.

```text
Read the supporting docs, spike findings and implementation beads. Claimed and synced **`hv-3x8.9.1`** for our design work; no code changes.

## Current interface baseline

| Interface | Recorded intent |
|---|---|
| `bee spawn <kind> <task-id>...` | Create a spawn request; don’t launch a process or claim its tasks. Return without waiting. |
| `bee status <spawn-id>` | Explain the request, linked-task readiness and execution outcome. Currently specified as Beads-only. |
| `colony wake` | Register a repository with the system-wide Colony; not start the daemon itself. Exact contract unfinished. |
| Close the spawn bead | End the request; Colony stops any running bee and releases unfinished claims. |

Daemon startup/shutdown, repository removal and runtime inspection commands are **not settled**.

## Constraints worth preserving

- **Request ≠ execution:** accepting a spawn does not mean a bee is running.
- **Repository ≠ worktree:** configuration, tracker selection and execution directory are separate concerns.
- Bees survive Colony restarts; replacement executions retain the request’s identity.
- All remaining open tasks must be ready before launch.
- `bee status` needs scheduling information, but currently cannot ask Colony. We must choose how Colony publishes that information—or revisit that restriction.
- Detached launches were demonstrated; complete adoption and descendant cleanup remain unverified.

Key references:
- `docs/agent-identity-scope.md:85` — configuration and command intent.
- `docs/harness-capabilities.md:35` — launch/recovery acceptance contract.
- `docs/beads-integration.md:29` — selected tracker endpoint, independent of execution cwd.

## Start with a concrete routing question

You’re in a feature worktree and request a bee for a task.

**Should the bee start in the canonical worktree and arrange its own working worktree, or inherit the caller’s worktree?**

My starting recommendation: **register repositories, not individual worktrees; launch from the canonical worktree, with worktree selection left to the bee’s workflow.** That keeps a queued request independent of a caller’s temporary checkout. An explicit execution-directory option should exist only if we have a concrete need.
```

```text
I’d aim for **two small interfaces**:

- **`bee`** — request work and inspect or cancel those requests.
- **`colony`** — operate the daemon and control which repositories it schedules.

This is a sketch, not an agreed spec.

## Bee

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `bee spawn <kind> <task-id>... [--cwd <dir>]` | Create a request; return its spawn ID and bee identity immediately. |
| `bee status <spawn-id>` | Show tasks, readiness, execution state and outcome. |
| `bee list` | List requests for the current repository, including queued and running work. |
| `bee stop <spawn-id>` | Close the request; Colony stops its execution and releases unfinished claims. |

**Spawn and status are already planned.** List and stop are proposed conveniences. Stop would wrap request closure—not directly kill a PID.

The **spawn ID is the durable handle**, including before launch and across retries. A running process is not the handle.

## Colony

| Command | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `colony start` | Start the system-wide daemon. |
| `colony stop` | Stop the daemon, leaving detached bees alive. |
| `colony status` | Show daemon health, registered repositories and scheduling activity. |
| `colony wake` | Register/resume scheduling for the current repository. |
| `colony sleep` | Pause that repository’s scheduling; proposed to leave running bees alone. |

Only **wake’s registration intent** is established; these exact commands and semantics remain proposals. We may need a foreground `run` entry point for a service manager, but shouldn’t design a whole service-management framework.

## Shared conventions

- Human-readable output by default; `--json` for automation.
- Repository context and tracker selection stay separate from execution location.
- `bee spawn --cwd` controls **where the harness starts**, accepts any existing directory, and defaults to the canonical worktree.
- Logs remain outside Beads. Whether access needs `bee logs` / `colony logs` or just reported file locations is undecided.
- Status must distinguish recorded state from live observations—the current Beads-only requirement needs reconciliation.

That gives us **three distinct lifecycles** to design: the daemon, repository scheduling, and each spawn request/execution. Stopping one should not implicitly mean stopping all three.
```

```text
**No—Colony doesn’t inherently need to read `bees.toml`.** It needs launch instructions and whatever scheduling policy it owns.

The useful distinction is **resolving configuration** versus **constructing a harness invocation**.

### Three possible designs

| Design | Bee submits | Colony does |
|---|---|---|
| **Named kind** | Kind name plus configuration reference | Reads configuration, resolves kind, constructs invocation |
| **Resolved recipe** | Harness, model, effort, prompt, extra arguments | Validates recipe, constructs invocation |
| **Prepared command** | Executable and complete argv | Executes it |

I’d favour the **middle option**, not turning Bee into a generator of complete harness commands.

### Resolved recipe versus named kind

| Concern | Resolved recipe | Named kind |
|---|---|---|
| **Overrides** | `--config` is resolved entirely by Bee | Must convey the configuration source to Colony |
| **Queued work** | Keeps the settings chosen when requested | Configuration edits can change pending work |
| **Disposable files** | Original TOML can disappear afterward | Configuration must remain available at launch |
| **Request size/control** | Larger contract; more fields a producer can get wrong | Smaller request; Colony controls interpretation |
| **Colony complexity** | No configuration discovery or kind lookup | Owns discovery, lookup and configuration failures |
| **Changing pending work** | Requires changing/replacing the recipe | Editing configuration can affect subsequent launches |

The disposable-file benefit applies to the TOML itself—not scripts, skills or other files referenced by the recipe.

### The asynchronous failure concern

You’re right that more supplied fields create more opportunities for mistakes. But there are two different failure classes:

- **Malformed recipe:** Bee can catch this synchronously using a shared schema. Colony checks the same contract when reading Beads, because requests are external input.
- **Unusable invocation:** unavailable model, unsupported effort, bad extra flag, missing executable or credentials. These can fail at launch **under either design**. Looking up a kind name doesn’t make its configuration executable.

Keeping harness-specific argument construction in Colony reduces the first design’s brittleness: Bee expresses intent; Colony’s harness adapter translates it.

### When would Colony read configuration?

Only if we choose behavior that requires it:

- Resolve bee kinds at launch time.
- Read Colony-owned policy, such as concurrency limits.
- Re-evaluate configuration-dependent admission rules at launch.

Those policies don’t necessarily belong in the same file as bee definitions.

**My leaning:** Bee reads `bees.toml` and submits a resolved, declarative recipe. Colony validates and dispatches it through its harness adapter—without discovering or rereading bee-kind configuration.
```

````text
**I’d keep cron outside Colony initially.** There are two different kinds of scheduling:

- **Timer:** decides when to **request work**.
- **Colony:** decides when an existing request is **ready to execute**, subject to readiness and capacity.

The flow stays simple:

```mermaid
flowchart LR

J --> B["bee spawn"]
B --> Q["Spawn bead with full recipe"]
Q --> C["Awake colony"]
C --> P["Detached process"]

The timer needs no harness knowledge. It invokes Bee, which reads configuration and prepares the recipe. Configuration changes affect **future requests**, not already-queued recipes.

### Stress cases

1. **Recurring work needs recurring task beads.**  
   Reusing a completed task won’t rerun it: under our existing rules, closed tasks are satisfied. A small job script can create the occurrence’s task and call `bee spawn`.

2. **The colony might be asleep.**  
   Creating the request still succeeds; execution waits. If the job should wake the colony, its automation explicitly invokes `colony wake`—Bee doesn’t secretly do so.

3. **The previous occurrence might still be running.**  
   Whether the next tick creates another request or skips it is the recurring job’s policy. Colony still handles execution capacity, but shouldn’t invent the meaning of overlapping occurrences.

I wouldn’t build another Hive tool yet. Start with cron/launchd and a small script; extract something only when repeated usage demonstrates the need.

Your direction does concentrate harness-specific changes in Bee. I’d separate:

- **Triage labels:** requested harness, model, bee kind.
- **Executable recipe:** executable, argv array, environment, cwd.
- **Display command:** derived from that recipe—not a second executable representation.

That prevents `model=sonnet`, the argv and a stored command string from becoming three contradictory sources of truth. Colony consumes a generic process recipe while owning readiness, dispatch, process tracking and lifecycle—not harness flags.

**Recurrence only needs to move into Colony if managing schedules becomes a core product capability.** Merely having a daemon already running isn’t a compelling reason to add calendars, missed-run policy and recurring-job state to it.
````

```text
A separate Colony config could still specify:

- At most **1 bee using a particular expensive model**.

The request already carries the kind and recipe attributes needed to apply those limits. Reading the launch definitions isn’t necessary.

### The important override rule

**A request’s `bee --config` must not implicitly replace Colony’s scheduling policy.**

Otherwise someone testing a prompt could accidentally change concurrency for the entire repository. Bee resolves its selected configuration; Colony reads its own policy source—probably the canonical configuration.

Also, a kind limit and a cost-related limit are different:
- `researcher <= 2` limits that named kind.
- An expensive-model limit applies even if an override selects that model under another kind.

We needn’t implement both immediately, but shouldn’t mistake one for the other.

### `max` is straightforward; `min` needs a meaning

A maximum limits **live executions**, not queued requests. Bees continuing after their colony sleeps still consume capacity.

But a minimum could mean:
```

````text
Yes, this is coherent. **Bee submits a parameterized request; Colony builds and dispatches the invocation using registered templates.** Harness-specific knowledge lives in configuration rather than application code.

That’s a shift from “Bee supplies the complete recipe,” but it still achieves your **one place to change harness options** goal.

### How it would work

1. **`colony wake`** loads canonical configuration: known kinds, launch templates and scheduling limits.
2. **Bee** reads configuration, selects a kind and applies request-specific overrides.
3. The spawn bead carries **kind + chosen parameter values + tasks + execution cwd**.
4. **Colony** checks capacity, selects the appropriate template, substitutes parameters and launches.
5. An explicit configuration update can register another kind without changing existing kinds.

Request overrides change launch parameters—not Colony’s limits or templates.

### The main snag: harness overrides

With your example, overriding `worker.harness` to `codex` changes the executable but leaves the **Claude-shaped argument template** attached to `worker`.

There are two coherent choices:

- **Harness fixed per kind:** your per-kind recipe arrangement works.
- **Harness overridable:** select the template by harness, independently of the kind.

For the second, a tidier sketch would be:

```toml
[kind.worker]
harness = "claude"
model = "opus"
effort = "low"
min = 0
max = 10

[harness.claude]
executable = "claude"
args = ["--model", "{{ model }}", "--effort", "{{ effort }}", "--yolo"]
```

*Illustrative configuration syntax, not a validated harness invocation.*

Here, **kind controls defaults and scheduling; harness controls invocation syntax**. Multiple kinds can share the same harness template.

### Why an argument array matters

Keep executable and argument tokens separate rather than rendering a shell command string. That avoids making quoting, spaces and shell interpretation part of your configuration language.

Your scout example also references `effort` without defining it. Template validation should expose that missing value, rather than silently producing an empty argument.

### Two consequences worth keeping visible

- **Same file does not mean same snapshot.** Colony reads on wake; Bee might read after an edit. A new kind therefore needs that explicit configuration-update operation before Colony can execute it.
- **Queued requests still depend on Colony’s templates.** Capturing parameter values fixes the requested model/effort, but updating a template can change how pending requests execute. That may be desirable—just different from a fully captured recipe.

My leaning: **this design is workable**, with separate kind defaults/limits and harness templates if harness overrides are supported. Colony becomes a configurable launcher, not merely a raw process dispatcher; that’s still a small, understandable responsibility.
````

title: Add bee kinds discovery with required kind descriptions
description:
Problem
During the first live Bee/Colony use, the caller could list submitted requests but could not discover which bee kinds were available. Agents need to discover who they can delegate to before choosing a kind. Kind configuration currently contains harness, model, effort and prompt, but no structured description.

User direction, 8 October 2026
Use bee kinds as the proposed discovery command. Every bee kind definition in canonical bees.toml must have a required description explaining its role and when to choose it. The user cited Codex subagent descriptions as the model: descriptions help the requesting agent select whom to delegate to; the full prompt supplies the selected bee's instructions.
Default bee kinds output should list the available kind names and their descriptions. Full prompts should not be exposed by default. Provide explicit verbosity/detail flag(s) for callers who want to inspect the full prompt; exact flag names and verbosity levels remain implementation choices.
Have the paired Bee help runbook direct agents to run discovery straight away. Consultations, reviews and implementation all use the same Bee mechanism.

Scope
Add kind discovery using the repository's canonical bees.toml and the existing repository/config resolution. design:
Settled discovery design — ct, 8 October 2026

Purpose
Visibility controls guidance: which bee kinds an agent is shown when choosing whom to delegate to. It is not a permission or runtime enforcement mechanism. An agent may still spawn a kind that discovery does not show. This deliberately supports testing and flexible workflows. Do not add visibility-based restrictions to spawn, retry, dispatch or execution; existing independent admission rules still apply.

Caller context
bee kinds --as <kind> explicitly selects the caller perspective and takes priority over BR_AGENT_NAME. Otherwise use BR_AGENT_NAME when present. With neither, apply no caller-specific policy and show all non-hidden kinds. Match kind names, independently of harness/model/version. The runtime already injects BR_AGENT_NAME from recipe.kind; do not derive caller kind from a model or from the target of a drone review.

TOML API
Each kind requires its description and may declare hidden, allow or deny:
- hidden defaults to false and supplies the ordinary visibility baseline for that target kind.
- allow and deny are mutually exclusive lists on the caller kind, naming target kinds.
- No allow/deny: show all non-hidden kinds.
- allow present: show exactly the listed kinds, INCLUDING kinds marked hidden. Explicit allow wins over hidden.
- deny present: show non-hidden kinds except the listed kinds. Deny does not expose hidden kinds.
- allow = []: show no kinds. deny = []: show the ordinary non-hidden baseline.
- #self is the sole special selector and expands to the caller kind. deny = ["#self"] hides that kind from itself; allow = ["#self", "honeybee"] explicitly includes it. There is no additional automatic self-hiding rule.
- Both allow and deny on one caller kind are a configuration error.

Examples (fragments; required existing fields omitted)
[kinds.drone]
hidden = true

[kinds.librarian]
allow = ["honeybee", "drone"]
# A librarian sees honeybee and drone, despite drone being hidden.

[kinds.reviewer]
deny = ["#self"]
# A reviewer sees non-hidden kinds other than reviewer.

Inspection and output
Default output remains concise names and required descriptions; prompts are omitted. --all bypasses discovery filtering, including hidden and caller policy, for intentional inspection. Verbosity/detail options independently control how much information is printed; full prompts require explicit opt-in. Preserve equivalent human and JSON visibility semantics. Detailed per-kind inspection is useful for configuring agents; exact detail/verbosity spelling can be finalized during implementation.

Reference and rationale
The user supplied /Users/ct/dev/projects/millhouse.spool/spools/harnesses/README.md around line 337 as the reference for mutually exclusive caller-owned allow/deny sets. Reuse that simple idea, not its Clojure configuration, alias-resolution inheritance or identity-history machinery.
User correction: "allow wins over hidden. That makes hidden simple, but overrides specific." The intention is guidance, not runtime enforcement, so invisible targets remain spawnable for testing and flexible workflows.

title: Make Bee help a concise shared agent runbook
description:
Problem
The first live Bee/Colony use required the caller to piece together AGENTS.md, CLI help and repository guides. Bee's current top-level help mostly enumerates commands/flags, whereas Honeycomb help supplies a concise agent workflow and common flows. Shared Bee usage guidance should ship with Bee so every project inherits it.

User direction and correction, 8 October 2026
Agents are already familiar with subagents. Nudge them to use Bee as their subagent system and provide the commands and short operational runbook in the same CLI help. This must not become a deep manual on the Bee system. There is one Bee mechanism for consultations, reviews and implementation; do not invent "lightweight consultation" versus "fully managed work" paths. The desired repository instruction is essentially to run Bee help for subagent work, plus genuinely repository-specific choices.

Scope
Model Bee help after Honeycomb: a short entry workflow, focused command examples and progressive detail in subcommand help. Direct agents to discover available bee kinds immediately, using hv-3x8.18, before selecting whom to delegate to. Explain the existing path for defining/linking the deliverable, submitting a request, Colony executing it, checking progress and retrieving the delivered answer. Make required execution prerequisites and next steps discoverable without a documentation hunt; do not introduce a second execution model. Clarify relevant option semantics, including whether --prompt replaces or supplements kind instructions, from the implementation.
Consolidate generic Bee operational guidance into CLI help and simplify Hive's AGENTS.md to the help entry point plus repository-specific role/routing and policy. Preserve existing ownership and permissions; no runtime lifecycle redesign is authorized by this task.

title: Spike: harness identity hook contracts (Claude Code, Codex, Pi)
description:

Per harness, establish:
- Hook/extension entry point and when it fires (startup, resume, clear, compact; subagent start).
- Payload fields: session id, model, effort/thinking level. Known so far: Codex SessionStart input is {session_id, transcript_path, cwd, hook_event_name, model, permission_mode, source} and output accepts only hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (vendored codex-rs/hooks/src/schema.rs); Claude effort availability is unknown.

notes:
## Verified harness identity contracts — hv-3x8.2

Research-only spike; no production modules, dependencies or repository docs added. Probed disposable configs/sessions and sentinels on 2026-10-02/03 UTC. O = observed on installed harness; S = inspected installed bundle or version-matched source; U = not live-verified. Source-backed lifecycle results are NOT represented as runtime captures.

Versions/provenance:
- Claude Code `2.1.287 (Claude Code)` (`claude --version` at probe start), native binary `/Users/ct/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.287`; bundled JS inspected via strings. All captured conversation/subagent records report version 2.1.287. The default CLI auto-updated to 2.1.288 by review time; that release is NOT covered by this matrix. Reproduce using the pinned 2.1.287 binary, whose --version was rechecked. Not a docs-only result.
- Codex `codex-cli 0.160.0` (`codex --version`). Source tag `rust-v0.160.0`, tag object `79b1b666f2e8551f8abbbca34957227f67f3f553`, commit `a956835d020762cb2b570053af06f643a11c0ecc`, fetched read-only through GitHub API. Existing vendor HEAD `e597169e9a783156e50ae9765d891a3dd74df064` is older and omits `fork`; it must NOT be used as the installed contract.
- Pi `1.0.0` (`pi --version`), installed `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` at `/Users/ct/.pi/agent/install/releases/1.0.0/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`. Agents checkout's 0.99.1 package is not the installed release.

### Capability matrix

| Capability | Claude Code 2.1.287 | Codex 0.160.0 | Pi 1.0.0 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entry point | Command hook in settings/plugin `hooks.SessionStart`; JSON stdin/stdout (O). | Command hook in `$CODEX_HOME/hooks.json` (`{"hooks":{...}}`); JSON stdin/stdout (O). Inline config/plugin sources also supported (S). | TS extension `pi.on("session_start", (event, ctx) => ...)`, loaded with `-e` or normal extension discovery (O/S). No JSON stdin hook. |
| Startup/resume/fork | SessionStart source `startup`/`resume`/`fork` observed. Resume same UUID; fork new UUID (O). | SessionStart source `startup`/`resume`/`fork` observed on first turn. Resume same root id; fork new root id (O). Hook dispatch is deferred until an agent turn, not just process launch (S). | Startup event; runtime switch emits `session_shutdown` then `session_start` reason `resume`/`fork`; same id on resume, new id on fork (O). Initial disposable RPC process reported startup; use ctx id, not reason alone, to resolve identity. |
| Clear/new | SessionEnd `clear`, rotates session UUID, then SessionStart `clear` (S; live TUI capture unavailable). | InitialHistory::Cleared creates a new root thread/session id and queues SessionStart `clear` (S; live TUI unavailable). | `/new` / RPC `new_session` is the clear-equivalent: shutdown/start reason `new`, new id (O). No core `/clear`. |
| Compaction | Reuses current session; SessionStart `compact` after compaction, in addition to compact hooks (S; live unavailable). | Replaces history in same Session; queues SessionStart `compact` for next dispatch, no identity rotation (S; live unavailable). | `session_before_compact` -> `session_compact`; same id; NO `session_start` (O). |
| Subagent start | Agent tool (formerly Task) emits `SubagentStart`, not a fresh root SessionStart. `session_id` remains parent; separate `agent_id`, `agent_type`; transcript_path is parent (O). | ThreadSpawn from `collaborationspawn_agent` emits `SubagentStart`, not SessionStart. `session_id` is ROOT identity; `agent_id` is child thread; transcript_path is child (O/S). Internal/synthetic subagents skipped (S). | No core subagent event. Separate child Pi process gets its own startup event/id and inherits parent env (O). Existing agents extension spawns such processes (S; plugin itself not live-tested). |
| Model/effort | SessionStart model optional (S) and ABSENT under --model haiku, settings pin, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, --effort low (O). Effort absent at SessionStart; optional model-gated field on tool-context hooks (S), not observed on Haiku. Compact callsite supplies model (S). | SessionStart includes resolved `model`; no effort/thinking field (O/S). transcript_path nullable by schema (S). | `ctx.model?.provider/id`, `ctx.thinkingLevel` (optional by types); reasoning model high, non-reasoning off; high->low change observed (O/S). Not event payload fields. |
| Environment injection | `CLAUDE_ENV_FILE` in SessionStart points to per-session hook shell script. Exports reach subsequent main AND subagent Bash calls; single-quoted special characters round-trip (O). Not a parent process.env mutation or a SubagentStart env channel. | No env/env-file output channel in hook schema (S). Static handler env affects hook process only (S). Launcher env still inherited (O). Native scent needs explicit --actor prompt guidance. | Mutation of process.env at session_start reaches pi.exec, model bash, RPC bash and a separately spawned Pi process (O). |
| Prompt injection | `{hookSpecificOutput:{hookEventName:"SessionStart",additionalContext:"..."}}` produces hook_additional_context attachment before user prompt (O). Bundle maps it into meta role=user message wrapped by system-reminder, NOT a true system/developer role (S; provider body not captured). | Same output channel; separate role=developer input_text message, tagged hooks.additional_context, observed in rollout (O/S). | Stable composable identity: return `{systemPrompt: event.systemPrompt + identity}` on every before_agent_start; later handlers receive the composed prompt. Leading system prompt (provider adapter rendered developer for fake OpenAI model), not a reminder attachment (O; composition verified in the follow-up below). |
| Parent env inheritance | HIVE_AGENT_NAME/SESSION/PARENT sentinels visible in SessionStart, SubagentStart, main Bash and subagent Bash (O). | HIVE_AGENT_NAME/SESSION/PARENT sentinels visible in SubagentStart hook; name also in all captured root events (O). Command runner inherits env + configured additions (S). | HIVE_AGENT_* sentinels in extension and subprocesses; parent-only mutation inherited by separate child (O). |

### Exact boundaries and implications

Claude:
- Observed minimal SessionStart keys are `session_id, transcript_path, cwd, hook_event_name, source`. Resume/fork add `seconds_since_last_response, context_tokens, prompt_cache_likely_expired, estimated_cache_write_usd`. Missing model/effort means ABSENT, not JSON null. Schema's optional fields are not startup guarantees.
- SessionStart output hookEventName is case-sensitive. Lowercase `sessionstart` produced a non-blocking hook error and dropped context; exact `SessionStart` worked.
- SessionStart env file is `session-env/<sid>/sessionstart-hook-N.sh`; subsequent hook processes (including SubagentStart) did NOT receive CLAUDE_ENV_FILE. Script contents are collected and applied by Bash execution (S); they do not prove arbitrary harness subprocess env mutation. Quote generated values as shell data. Single-quoted spaces, double quotes, literal $HOME, backticks and a backslash round-tripped byte-for-byte in both main and subagent Bash (see env snapshots). Unquoted expansion was not live-tested.
- Native Agent subagents share parent-session env exports. Root-session-only identity resolution cannot give each native subagent its own exported actor; a SubagentStart prompt may use agent_id, but that does not change per-session shell env. Separate nested CLI processes are different from native subagents.
- `--init-only` is zero-model startup probe, but reports source startup even with --resume/--fork-session. Real -p resume/fork probes were required; do not use init-only to infer lifecycle sources.

Codex:
- Exact SessionStart keys are `session_id, transcript_path, cwd, hook_event_name, model, permission_mode, source`; no turn_id. SubagentStart adds turn_id/agent_id/agent_type. Root session_id deliberately shared by descendant threads in 0.160.0, not a unique child conversation id.
- Output wire is camelCase. SessionStart universal keys also allow continue/stopReason/suppressOutput/systemMessage; hookSpecificOutput carries hookEventName/additionalContext. No env/environment key. Inheritance alone cannot bind an HIVE_AGENT_SESSION in native Codex tools; do not claim prompt guidance exports it.
- Observed exec hook trust gating: without `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`, hooks were skipped with warnings. Bypass was used only with disposable probe-owned hooks; production installation/launch must make an explicit trust decision.
- Initial subagent-negative probe had SubagentStart unregistered. Corrected registration DID fire it. Collaboration subagents are NOT a blind spot; only internal/synthetic sources are skipped (S). Earlier vendor-based claims are superseded.

Pi:
- session_start event has `{type,reason,previousSessionFile?}`; session id/model/thinking come from ctx, not JSON stdin. New/resume/fork replacement in RPC emitted session_start/resources_discover TWICE; confirmed double rebind callsites in installed RPC/core. Make identity resolution idempotent by current session id; do not infer two sessions from two callbacks. This duplication claim is RPC-specific, not proven for TUI.
- before_agent_start input has prompt, images?, readonly systemPrompt, mutable systemPromptOptions. Returning systemPrompt replaces the complete prompt for that run; append/preserve prior text. Override observed on every provider request in a tool loop, absent from persisted JSONL and compaction summary request. Reinject on each agent run. model_select and thinking_level_select can refresh best-effort metadata after startup (S; thinking change O).
- Built-in model Bash gets PI_SESSION_ID/PI_SESSION_FILE/PI_PROVIDER/PI_MODEL/PI_REASONING_LEVEL resolved per call. RPC/user Bash did not receive those automatic session vars, but DID receive process.env mutations. Do not conflate those paths.
- Pi probe used a local canned OpenAI-compatible provider; zero real-model work for its lifecycle, compaction, prompt or tool-env tests.

Actual disposable-session payloads, paths shortened only; UUIDs kept consistent. These are samples, not guaranteed full schemas.

## Pi prompt composition clarification — ct, 2026-10-03

Pi prompt persistence is not an unresolved identity limitation. Each before_agent_start handler reads the current composed event.systemPrompt and appends its own contribution. The next handler sees that returned prompt. Repeating the same composition on each agent run maintains stable identity and preserves other extensions; the per-run return value is normal API mechanics, not evidence that identity disappears between turns. A renderer that owns the base prompt runs before appenders.

Verified against installed Pi 1.0.0: extensions/runner.js:1115-1160 renders the current options for each handler and applies each returned systemPrompt as the next forceSystemPrompt. agent-session.js:1555 starts each run from base options; :1314 projects the override across provider requests and :1373 clears run options on completion. This does not undermine stable per-run composition. Compaction uses its own prompt, as originally recorded; the identity contribution is re-established for subsequent agent runs.

Focused runtime evidence: node /tmp/hive-pi-prompt-composition.mjs exercised the actual installed ExtensionRunner.emitBeforeAgentStart and buildSystemPrompt with two probe handlers across three independent calls. All 29 assertions passed: the second handler saw the first contribution; the base prompt and both contributions survived in order; exactly one copy of each contribution appeared; outputs were identical across runs; caller base options were unchanged. This probes the installed runner with minimal context, not a new full CLI/provider lifecycle test. Earlier spike provider captures remain the evidence for tool-loop requests.

Practical reference: /Users/ct/dev/projects/agents/pi/extensions/system-prompt/index.ts:301-331 rebuilds the owned prompt with cached identity every before_agent_start; package.json loads this renderer first. Downstream extensions compose after it. The existing cross-extension integration test was inspected as an example, not newly executed. That checkout declares Pi 0.99.1 dependencies; installed-runner verification used Pi 1.0.0. No changes to the agents repository or Hive production code.

The original every-run append guidance was correct. Calling it a design gap, and the later spoken phrase “the prompt is temporary,” overstated the limitation. ct considers this normal composition pattern sufficient; no extra prompt-persistence mechanism is requested. RPC duplicate session-start callbacks and session ancestry semantics remain separate findings.


## Current attribution decision — ct, 2026-10-03

Native Claude Code Agent/Task subagents are supported in the planned identity system through the same explicit-attribution approach as Codex. This supersedes the brief exclusion recorded earlier in this discussion.

- Pi: process environment plus stable composable identity in the system prompt on each run.
- Primary Claude Code sessions: SessionStart environment exports plus identity context.
- Native Codex sessions/subagents and native Claude Code subagents: identity context with explicit `br --actor <own-friendly-name>` on every tracker mutation. Share the explicit-attribution guidance; keep event parsing and context delivery in the harness-specific adapters.
- Native child identity uses the distinct agent_id; parent/root session_id alone cannot distinguish siblings. Preserve the parent identity and shared environment. An explicit child actor overrides inherited BD_ACTOR for that command; do not rewrite the session-wide environment file for a native child.
- Separately launched CLI processes, including colony bees, retain launcher-provided environment support. Identity attribution support for native subagents does not make them colony-managed spawn beads.

1. Direct: a short-lived Python parent used subprocess.Popen(argv, cwd=probe_dir, env=probe_env, stdin=DEVNULL, stdout=stdout_file, stderr=stderr_file, start_new_session=True), then exited immediately. All three native harnesses remained running with PPID=1 and PGID=PID and completed the requested tool call plus both prompt markers. Observed leaders: Claude 4220, Codex 4222, Pi/Node 4221. Their launcher PIDs were already gone. This verifies survival of parent exit without a terminal, not just backgrounding while a parent remains alive.
2. Detached waiting supervisor: the launcher exited after spawning a new-session supervisor; the supervisor waited for its harness and wrote process/exit receipts. This preserved actual wait returncodes after the launcher exited. Supervisor stdin was /dev/null; logs were independent files; it set SIGHUP ignored (nohup-style), although a harness can install its own handler. All native success/signal/flag/sandbox runs in this arrangement survived launcher exit while doing work.

Use a new session/no controlling TTY and persistent log files; merely nohup or unref is not a child-tree cleanup strategy. Never keep colony-owned pipe readers or inherited terminal input as the only log path. The directly orphaned process's exit status cannot later be obtained by a restarted, non-parent colony with waitpid: persist an exit receipt with an independently surviving waiter/supervisor, or treat disappearance without a receipt as unknown. Receipt design was explored, not implemented in Hive.

Liveness probes used kill(pid, 0), confirmed by ps showing PID/PPID/PGID/state. A PID being present is not task success and does not prove tools are gone. Production persistence must identify the same process (birth/start time and machine boot identity, not PID alone), handle zombies and permission errors appropriately, and distinguish known completion from missing exit evidence. No PID-identity persistence implementation is part of this spike.

### Observed exit/output matrix

- Normal native success: all 0; Claude final result is_error=false/terminal_reason=completed, Codex turn.completed, Pi final stopReason=stop and agent_settled.
- Invalid native options: Claude unknown --hv-3x8-3-invalid -> 1; Codex exec unknown option -> 2; Pi --mode invalid -> 1. stdout empty; diagnostics/usage on stderr. Capture stderr from spawn time, including failures before any session/log file exists.
- Deterministic local HTTP 400 HV3X83_LOCAL_FAILURE: Claude --bare --output-format json -> 1 with error result ON STDOUT, empty stderr. Its result surprisingly has subtype=success but is_error=true, terminal_reason=api_error, api_error_status=400. Do not classify Claude by subtype alone. Codex --json -> 1, stdout error plus turn.failed events, stderr only its stdin notice.
- Native Pi same HTTP 400: text mode -> 1, empty stdout, error on stderr; JSON mode -> 0, empty stderr, assistant stopReason=error/errorMessage in JSONL. This verifies the documented JSON-mode exception: CLI exit 0 alone is NOT success. Read settled/event outcomes as well as exit status. This is especially important if colony chooses JSON progress logs.
- Native Claude/Pi SIGTERM -> explicit process exit 143; both killed the active long-running Python tool. Native Codex SIGTERM -> wait returncode -15 (shell convention 143), but its tool stayed alive and reparented to PID 1.
- SIGKILL of each native harness -> wait returncode -9 (shell convention 137), and each left its tool alive. No final completion/error event is guaranteed on a kill.
- Native Claude/Pi SIGHUP -> 129 and active tool gone. Codex's HUP probe subsequently completed 0 with tool gone rather than a signal-coded exit; it had yielded the long-running exec task and reported it still running before normal teardown. This does NOT prove SIGHUP is a graceful stop command or that it caused teardown. Use TERM/KILL with owned descendant cleanup instead.
- Read-only/capability refusal can still finish 0. A denied tool operation and a failed harness/API invocation are different outcomes; do not assume all tool errors make the CLI fail.

Representative tree observations before/after native SIGTERM: Claude leader 92556 PGID 92552, tool 92672 PGID 92672 -> tool absent; Pi leader 92557 PGID 92554, tool 92699 PGID 92699 -> absent; Codex leader 92555 PGID 92553, tool 92735 PGID 92735 -> still alive with PPID 1. SIGKILL survivors were Claude tool 93367, Pi tool 93385 and Codex tool 93404; they were explicitly removed by SIGKILL to their recorded tool process groups. ps later confirmed every recorded harness and probe PID absent.

### Reaping a bee and its children

All three native harnesses put tool work in a separate process group/session from the harness. Therefore kill(-bee_pid, signal) alone is insufficient even when the bee was launched as its own session leader. Claude/Pi's cooperative TERM handlers cleaned the tested foreground tool; Codex TERM did not. SIGKILL bypasses cleanup for every harness.

A verified bounded recipe for these probes is: retain/snapshot owned descendant PIDs and their process groups WHILE the leader is alive; signal the leader with TERM; observe exit and descendant state; kill remaining recorded tool groups and the launch group; verify the recorded descendants are gone. Do not discover children only after killing the leader: the Codex/Pi examples were already adopted by PID 1. The probe's killpg(recorded_tool_pgid, SIGKILL) reaped the escaped tools, and final ps verification found no recorded live processes. This verifies the probe tree, not arbitrary self-daemonizing grandchildren or processes that escape ownership between snapshots. A process-tree snapshot is not a race-free containment boundary; reliable arbitrary descendants require an external ownership/containment mechanism or supervisor that tracks them independently. Choose that policy in the colony lifecycle design rather than pretending a PID/PGID alone guarantees complete reap.

### Permission/sandbox inputs

- Codex: --sandbox read-only / workspace-write / danger-full-access. Read-only probe requested a harmless marker write; the agent reported operation not permitted and the marker remained absent. Its JSONL did not expose a command_execution result for the denied call, so this run is an accepted-flag/no-write observation, NOT independent proof of the sandbox's security enforcement. Success/environment probes used workspace-write. Use -c approval_policy="never" for an explicit noninteractive policy when retaining user config; exec's current no-interactive-approval behavior was sufficient in the isolated runs. --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox exists, but was not used and is not needed for the tested recipe.
- Claude: --permission-mode plan produced a model refusal without attempting the write; no marker existed. Plan is not an OS read-only sandbox. For a capability-restricted scout, --tools Read,Grep,Glob removes command/write tools; --permission-prompts none prevents headless approval waits; dontAsk denies operations not allowlisted. The verified environment/lifecycle probes instead used dontAsk, --tools Bash,Read and --allowedTools Bash in disposable directories; that unrestricted Bash capability is NOT a read-only recipe. acceptEdits enables edits; bypassPermissions/--dangerously-skip-permissions bypass gating. No bypass flag was used. An OS sandbox is still needed if arbitrary command-capable read-only enforcement is required.
- Pi: --tools read,grep,find,ls (with --no-extensions) removed bash/edit/write from native model-visible tools; the write request reported no write/shell capability and created no marker. This is tool capability restriction, NOT OS sandboxing. --approve/--no-approve governs trust/loading of project-local files, not filesystem permissions. Enabling bash or arbitrary extensions removes the read-only capability guarantee unless externally sandboxed.

### Installed PATH pi is Pies, not native Pi

/Users/ct/.local/bin/pi points to /Users/ct/dev/projects/agents/pies/pi-shim.ts. --help/--version report managed native Pi 1.0.0, but -p routes to a persistent Pies daemon running Pi SDK 0.99.1. Consequently --version alone does not identify the headless runtime. The installed shim was separately exercised on a private PIES_SOCKET=<evidence-dir>/pies.sock, never the default daemon hosting this conversation. Same model/thinking/repeated append options and shell env sentinels succeeded; parent exit survival succeeded.

Shim client TERM -> 143 after daemon settlement/lease release; recorded tool disappeared. Client KILL -> -9/137; the private daemon canceled that request and the tool disappeared in this run. However forced-client death has no settlement acknowledgement: disappearance/137 does not guarantee backend cleanup in general. Actual tool PPID was private daemon 93729, not the client; client PID/process-group tree cannot enumerate daemon-owned work. Do not kill a shared Pies daemon to reap one bee. Either select native Pi explicitly for a PID-owned bee, or use the shim's per-request cancellation/settlement contract and separately account for daemon health and cleanup. Private daemon status after probes: active=0, session leases=0; it was then stopped using only its private socket. The user's default daemon was untouched.

### Verification and retained evidence

29 final probe reports: 3 native successful launches, 3 direct orphaned launches, 3 native TERM, 3 native KILL, 3 native HUP, 3 invalid-option, 3 read-only/capability, 1 Codex default-env, 1 Pies success, 2 Pies TERM/KILL, 4 deterministic local-API errors (Pi text+JSON, Claude JSON, Codex JSON). All expected observations were inspected; deliberately induced failures are findings, not unfinished tests. One Codex error-probe setup attempt failed because its temporary CODEX_HOME did not exist; the directory was created and the actual API-failure case rerun successfully. No real credential or auth changes were made.

Baseline and final: qlock -w 180 /tmp/millstrand-test.lock bun run check passed (format/lint/all typechecks). Full suite: qlock -w 180 /tmp/millstrand-test.lock bun run test passed, 262 tests, 0 failures, 605 assertions, 22 files, 8.35s. Worktree git status is clean. No production code changed, so no new automated tests were added; the scope-specific tests are the live/manual launch probes and local deterministic failure probes. Interactive TTY sessions, native Claude --bg, Windows/Linux, arbitrary daemonized descendants, custom plugins/scent identity and actual bead mutation under sandbox remain explicitly unverified and were not required to claim these headless-launch acceptance criteria.

Local scratch evidence (temporary, not a substitute for the durable findings above): /var/folders/6w/lnly9x394flgz3q7zty955500000gn/T/hv-3x8.3-launch-rf8wj145, containing argv.json, stdout.log, stderr.log, report.json and process/exit receipts by case. Scripts: /tmp/hv-3x8.3-spike.py and /tmp/hv-3x8.3-error-probe.py. Launch env spec files were private and removed after use. All recorded harness/tool processes and the private Pies daemon were verified stopped.

References (moving online docs are subordinate to the installed versions and observed runs): https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless ; https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference ; https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions ; https://developers.openai.com/codex/noninteractive ; https://developers.openai.com/codex/cli/reference ; https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-reference ; https://pi.dev/docs/latest/cli ; https://pi.dev/docs/latest/cli-integration . Native Pi source corroboration: dist/modes/print-mode.js (JSON/text error status distinction and TERM/HUP), dist/core/tools/bash.js and dist/utils/shell.js (env inheritance, detached tool groups and signal cleanup). Installed Pies README and cli.ts corroborate client-vs-daemon and cancellation acknowledgement. Existing Hive scripts/beads-loop.ts is a waiting/inherited-stream launcher, not a detached process-tree supervisor; it was read but never run or modified.
Acceptance verification complete: canonical repository br show reports 22,689 characters of substantive final findings, including actual argv/env, observed process/exit outcomes and real tool-result evidence for all harnesses. All three acceptance items are checked from the 29 final probe reports and passing quality/test commands above. Reviewer confirmed the technical findings are supported and carefully bounded; its initial tracker finding came from the worktree-local stale database (open, 84-char original note), not the canonical tracker where this bead was claimed and updated. Canonical state is in_progress, assigned pi, owner ct with full durable evidence; no worktree-local bead mutation was performed.
Final review: reviewer rechecked the canonical tracker, confirmed substantive findings and all three checked acceptance items, withdrew the stale-worktree tracker finding, and reported no remaining technical closure blocker. Research spike complete; no application code or other beads were changed.

Historical reap/children language describes prior terminology or OS subprocess ownership, not a current Hive agent hierarchy or settled bee life enum. Use plain descriptions of stopping execution and process cleanup in downstream design; preserve the actual process-group findings and unresolved containment limits.

title: shared: identity and bee contract (env names, mintName, bees.toml schema)
description:
## Revised shared contract — extract what real consumers need

Current outcome summary: hv-3x8.9.1 design. Verbatim evidence: hv-3x8.17. Next implementation: hv-3x8.9.3.

Do not make this complete multi-consumer contract a preparatory blocker for hv-3x8.9.3. That user-authorized slice establishes the minimal manual request/config/launch shape, using only the shared code it actually needs. Reuse/extract that tested shape here when Bee and Scent require it; do not build a general configuration framework first.

Keep the agreed identity environment names and mintName scope from the prior description. Recipe, formula and scheduling policy are distinct: a recipe snapshots effective kind/harness/model/effort and launch context; a named harness formula supplies executable/argument syntax; kinds and colony policy carry non-preemptive maximums. There is no min field. Retry budget belongs in bees.toml with an explicit sensible default selected during its slice.

Both consumers use canonical bees.toml for different sections. Bee accepts CLI recipe-value overrides, no alternate config-file layering; Colony accepts transient formula/limit overrides only, stored with SQLite history and reset by wake from canonical config. Neither automatically synchronizes the other's overrides. A harness identifier cannot be limited to a fixed built-in union merely because the old scaffold used claude/codex/pi: a request may name an explicitly installed runtime formula unknown to Bee. Capability support remains independently verified by profile.

Parse inputs at entry and use a popular existing template engine for formulas, not custom interpolation code. Handlebars strict/plain-text rendering was researched; its lazy compilation needs eager syntax validation at config load. Exact TOML keys, template value schema and storage fields are to be proven in the vertical slice, not copied from the older illustrative schema below.

Keep shared minimal and preserve current only-shared package boundaries. Friendly identity attribution remains separate from best-effort harness/model/effort metadata, and native child IDs are not a Hive ancestry model.

## Historical prior scope — superseded where inconsistent above

Add the minimal contract both scent and bee/colony need, in @hive/shared. scent and bee/colony stay orthogonal and never import each other; this contract is their only shared surface, so add nothing either side does not clearly need.

- Env var names: HIVE_AGENT_NAME, HIVE_AGENT_SESSION, plus br's BD_ACTOR, BR_HARNESS, BR_MODEL, BR_AGENT_NAME.
- mintName(seed): deterministic 3-word adjective-adjective-noun name (~1e9 space; choose or inline word lists per the repo's tooling guidance). Sessions started directly seed it with the session id (so resume/compact keep the name); harness subagents use a distinct harness-provided agent key; bee supplies a fresh seed at spawn and reuses its identity on respawn.
- bees.toml schema + parser (Bun.TOML): users = [...] (configurable list of human names, e.g. ["ct"]; bee refuses any task assigned to one), [[bee]] name, description, systemPrompt, cli (claude|codex|pi), model, effort?, args = [] (escape hatch, array, may carry sandbox/read-only flags; there is no separate permissions field). Parse at the boundary and fail loudly on malformed files.

Friendly names ordinarily distinguish agents but carry no global uniqueness promise; harness, model and effort are separate best-effort agent attributes. Requester attribution identifies the human or agent that requested a bee, not a Hive parent-child hierarchy. Earlier HIVE_AGENT_PARENT proposals must be reconciled in hv-3x8.9.1/hv-3x8.12 rather than treated as an already-required field; this alignment does not invent a replacement environment variable. Preserve actual harness identifiers needed for attribution isolation.

Follow the typescript and testing skills. Final env names must follow the reconciled design and hooks evidence.

- [ ] Unit tests: mintName determinism and format; parser accepts valid files and rejects malformed ones
